title: Solid Mechanics
full_title: Advanced Solid Mechanics: Elasticity, Plasticity and Fracture
tagline: Stress and strain tensors, linear elasticity, energy methods, thick cylinders and rotating discs, thin-walled structures, plates, plasticity, fracture and composites
summary: Solid mechanics goes beyond bars, shafts and beams to the general theory of deformable solids. The course develops stress and strain in three dimensions, the equations of linear elasticity and their classical solutions, energy methods, thick cylinders and rotating discs, thin-walled aircraft-type structures, the bending of plates, plasticity and limit loads, linear-elastic fracture mechanics and the mechanics of composite laminates.
overview: Solid mechanics is the general theory of how deformable bodies carry load: how forces spread through a solid as stress, how the solid deforms as strain, and how the two are tied together by the material. The bar, shaft and beam formulas of [[mechanics-of-materials]] are special cases of this theory, each resting on an assumption about how the body deforms. This course drops those assumptions one at a time, so that you can analyse parts for which no handbook formula exists and judge when the handbook formulas are good enough.

The first three chapters build the machinery: the Cauchy stress tensor and the equilibrium equations, the small-strain tensor and compatibility, the generalised Hooke's law and the boundary-value problem of linear elasticity with its two-dimensional solutions by the Airy stress function, and the energy methods (Castigliano's theorems, virtual work, minimum potential energy and the Rayleigh–Ritz method) on which the finite element method is built. The next three apply it to classical structural forms: thick cylinders, shrink fits and rotating discs; thin-walled open and closed sections, shear flow and the shear centre; and the bending and buckling of thin plates.

The last three chapters leave linear elasticity behind. Plasticity covers yield criteria, flow rules, elastic–plastic bending and torsion and the limit (collapse) load of beams and frames. Fracture mechanics explains why cracked parts fail far below their yield strength and how the stress intensity factor, fracture toughness and the Paris law are used in damage-tolerant design. The course ends with the mechanics of fibre composite laminates: orthotropic plies, classical laminate theory and failure criteria.

The difficulty is less the mathematics — vectors, matrices, partial derivatives and a few ordinary differential equations, all covered in [Maths Atlas](/learn/maths/) — than keeping three kinds of equation apart: equilibrium (statics), compatibility (geometry) and the constitutive law (material). Every solution in the course is a combination of these three, and most mistakes come from confusing one with another or from forgetting a boundary condition. Work every example with that bookkeeping in mind, check limiting cases, and remember that real pressure vessels, rotors, aircraft structures and composite parts are designed to codes and checked by qualified engineers; the course teaches the principles behind those codes.
outcomes: Calculate the traction on any plane, the principal stresses and directions, and the maximum shear stress from a three-dimensional stress tensor.
Derive strains from a displacement field, check compatibility, and reduce strain-gauge rosette readings to principal strains and stresses.
Formulate the boundary-value problem of linear elasticity and solve plane problems with Airy stress functions.
Use Castigliano's theorems, the unit-load method and the Rayleigh–Ritz method to find deflections and redundant reactions.
Calculate stresses and displacements in thick cylinders, shrink fits and rotating discs with the Lamé solution.
Analyse thin-walled open and closed sections for unsymmetric bending, shear flow, shear centre and torsion.
Calculate deflections and stresses of rectangular and circular plates and the buckling stress of plates in compression.
Apply the Tresca and von Mises criteria, and find the collapse load of beams and frames by the plastic hinge method.
Calculate stress intensity factors, critical crack sizes and fatigue crack-growth lives for damage-tolerant design.
Compute the stiffness of a fibre-composite laminate with classical laminate theory and predict first-ply failure.

chapters.title: Stress and strain in three dimensions
chapters.summary: The Cauchy stress tensor and the equilibrium equations, the small-strain tensor and compatibility, principal values and strain-gauge rosettes.

chapters.title: Linear elasticity
chapters.summary: Generalised Hooke's law, the boundary-value problem of elasticity, plane stress and plane strain, and Airy stress functions.

chapters.title: Energy methods
chapters.summary: Strain energy, Castigliano's theorems, the principle of virtual work and the principle of minimum potential energy.

chapters.title: Thick cylinders and rotating discs
chapters.summary: The Lamé solution for thick-walled cylinders, shrink fits and the stresses in rotating discs.

chapters.title: Thin-walled structures
chapters.summary: Bending, shear and torsion of thin-walled open and closed sections, shear flow and the shear centre, and multicell box beams.

chapters.title: Bending of thin plates
chapters.summary: Kirchhoff plate theory, rectangular and circular plates under lateral load, and the buckling of plates.

chapters.title: Plasticity
chapters.summary: Yield criteria, flow rules and hardening, elastic–plastic bending and torsion, and limit analysis.

chapters.title: Fracture mechanics
chapters.summary: Stress intensity factors, energy release rate and fracture toughness, fatigue crack growth and damage-tolerant design.

chapters.title: Mechanics of composite laminates
chapters.summary: Orthotropic laminae, classical laminate theory and failure criteria for fibre composites.

history.title: Cauchy's concept of stress
history.detail: Augustin-Louis Cauchy presented to the Paris Academy of Sciences his theory of the state of stress at a point, described by six components acting on three planes; it was published in 1823 and developed in his *Exercices de mathématiques* (1827).

history.title: Kirchhoff's theory of plates
history.detail: Gustav Kirchhoff published the theory of thin elastic plates, with the boundary conditions that still bear his name, in the *Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik*.

history.title: Lamé's lectures on elasticity
history.detail: Gabriel Lamé's *Leçons sur la théorie mathématique de l'élasticité des corps solides*, the first book on the mathematical theory of elasticity, included the solution for a thick-walled cylinder under pressure.

history.title: Tresca's yield condition
history.detail: Henri Tresca reported to the French Academy experiments on the flow of metals under high pressure, from which the maximum-shear-stress yield criterion is named.

history.title: Castigliano's theorems
history.detail: Alberto Castigliano published *Théorie de l'équilibre des systèmes élastiques et ses applications*, setting out the energy theorems used to find deflections and redundant forces.

history.title: Von Mises yield criterion
history.detail: Richard von Mises proposed the yield condition based on the second invariant of the deviatoric stress, anticipated by Maksymilian Huber in 1904.

history.title: Griffith's theory of fracture
history.detail: A. A. Griffith's paper 'The phenomena of rupture and flow in solids' (*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A*) explained the low strength of glass by an energy balance on cracks.

history.title: The stress intensity factor
history.detail: George R. Irwin showed that the stress field near a crack tip is scaled by a single parameter, the stress intensity factor, and related it to the energy release rate (*Journal of Applied Mechanics*, 1957).

history.title: The J-integral
history.detail: James R. Rice introduced the path-independent J-integral for analysing cracks with plastic zones at the tip.

history.title: Tsai–Wu failure criterion
history.detail: Stephen W. Tsai and Edward M. Wu published a general tensor-polynomial strength criterion for anisotropic materials, widely used for fibre composite laminae.

references.title: Theory of Elasticity
references.authors: S. P. Timoshenko and J. N. Goodier
references.note: 3rd edition (McGraw-Hill). The classic text on stress functions, plane problems, thick cylinders, rotating discs and torsion.

references.title: Elasticity
references.note: 3rd edition (Springer). A modern, readable treatment of plane elasticity and Airy stress functions, with many solved problems.

references.title: Advanced Mechanics of Materials
references.authors: A. P. Boresi and R. J. Schmidt
references.note: 6th edition (Wiley). Bridges mechanics of materials and elasticity: energy methods, thick cylinders, shear centre, plates, fracture and plasticity at undergraduate level.

references.title: Theory of Plates and Shells
references.note: 2nd edition (McGraw-Hill). The standard reference for plate solutions and tables of deflection and moment coefficients.

references.title: Aircraft Structures for Engineering Students
references.note: 6th edition (Butterworth-Heinemann). Thin-walled open and closed sections, shear flow, structural idealisation and energy methods for aircraft structures.

references.title: The Mathematical Theory of Plasticity
references.note: Oxford University Press. The foundational text on yield criteria, flow rules and plastic boundary-value problems.

references.title: Fracture Mechanics: Fundamentals and Applications
references.note: 4th edition (CRC Press). Linear-elastic and elastic–plastic fracture mechanics, toughness testing and fatigue crack growth.

references.title: Mechanics of Composite Materials
references.note: 2nd edition (Taylor & Francis). Lamina stiffness, classical lamination theory and failure criteria.
